correspondence.finding: The chosen northern opening occupies a narrow upland collector descending southeast and south through cultivated mountain terrain. The image supports this opening as a geographic valley segment, without assigning a spring, a natural river source, or a name to the chosen vertex. Its upper tributary name remains unverified.

Cloud and shadow obscure the selected upper westward bend and its return toward the southgoing collector, beside a pale enlarged-water feature. The available image establishes the surrounding valley setting but does not establish the complete selected through-link and junction. The feature is not assigned a reservoir name, and no hydraulic route through it is inferred. This is the single remaining material geographic gap.

Below the unresolved upper setting, the selection follows the southgoing upland valley, then turns southeast along its footslope corridor. Small lateral valleys are geographically distinct from the selected collector; no names are inferred from imagery.

The selected valley continues south through the widening river corridor and its tributary meeting places. The broad valley and visible river segments correspond at ordinary corridor scale; the selected course remains the northern approach rather than the lateral western and eastern tributaries. FONAC names Río Grande del Sur as the upstream branch through Reitoca, Alubarén and part of La Venta, but does not fix exact reach-name transitions.

The selection passes the elongated middle-valley impoundment and continues into the downstream river corridor. The photographs show the receiving waterbody, its narrowed lower end and downstream valley. FONAC identifies José Cecilio del Valle, also called Nacaome, as the reservoir in this river system. This supports ordinary reservoir-passage correspondence, without claims about present operations, water levels or precise bank alignment.

The selected river continues south through a visible meandering corridor, turns west and southwest, and enters the wider settled and cultivated plain. The source depicts the river corridor across the intervening bends and joins. Small model shortcuts remain within this continuously depicted corridor and are not treated as separate missing hydraulic links.

The lower image shows the northeastern river approach meeting a separate northern approach beside the Nacaome settlement setting. The selected course continues southwest beyond their receiving confluence. FONAC independently identifies the Grande del Sur and Guacirope branches as joining at Nacaome; Guacirope is retained as a distinct joining branch, not substituted for the selected upper route.

The downstream course continues southwest through the cultivated coastal plain, then winds west through the broad coastal channel beside mangrove wetlands and rectilinear managed ponds. The selected endpoint is at the inner bay-side river opening in the Gulf of Fonseca setting, not at the open Pacific coast. Continuous geographic correspondence is visible through the lower meanders and receiving coastal water. No pond-crossing, presently active distributary, tidal boundary or current water-management route is inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen eastern ice-field opening and the continuous western bending glacier corridor.

The route continues across the ice into the directly labeled Marcus Baker Glacier and follows its broad westward trough to the glacier margin. The entire chosen opening and glaciated passage are geographically depicted; this is not evidence of a natural-river channel or an identified hydraulic route on or below the ice.

correspondence.component_scope: Western glacier edge and the south-then-west Glacier Fork valley.
correspondence.finding: The mapped glacier trough gives way to the stream corridor labeled Glacier Fork Knik River. The selected generalized path follows that valley southward, then westward along the northern margin of the large adjoining ice body. The glacier-to-valley transition and enclosed receiving corridor are continuously covered at ordinary scale. No exact present ice-front or river-bank position is assigned.

correspondence.component_scope: Glacier Fork foreland and the selected mainstem fragment junction.
correspondence.finding: The selected mainstem enters a single open proglacial foreland with channels, lake margins and the downstream braided Knik corridor. The overview and middle original depict that complete receiving setting and its westward outlet; the generalized path does not need to match a single active braid. The shared endpoint of mainstem fragments 2666 and 2667 lies in this foreland receiving corridor.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen southern ice-margin opening, elongated marginal lake, northern outlet and join to the mainstem.
correspondence.finding: The tributary begins along the western edge of the adjoining glacier, beside a narrow marginal water passage, and runs north through the mapped elongated lake and outlet setting. Lake Fork Knik River is directly labeled along this lake-margin corridor. The selected continuation turns northwest through the open foreland to its recorded confluence with the selected mainstem. Geographic correspondence of the opening, lake passage, outlet and receiving join is complete; no separate name is assigned to the lake itself.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower braided valley past the northern lakes and the southern mountain front.
correspondence.finding: The selected downstream route follows the broad continuously mapped braided belt repeatedly labeled Knik River. The lower original shows the selected corridor through its westward turn, the approach toward the Matanuska receiving flats and the channels crossing the Glenn Highway. Distinct nearby wetland channels and tributaries are not all renamed Knik River.

correspondence.component_scope: Common lower Knik–Matanuska estuarine receiving flats west of the Glenn Highway.
correspondence.finding: Both terminal positions retained by the core metadata were inspected against the lower original. The source endpoint is on the northern receiving-channel side, where Matanuska River is labeled, and the rendered endpoint is farther south at the adjacent tidal-water margin. Both occupy the same connected lower river/estuarine receiving setting. The rendered final segment and the source endpoint are described separately; the last aggregate stored position of tributary 2668 is not mistaken for the mainstem mouth. No exact bank, present tidal edge or separate hydraulic route is asserted.
